title: Technical writing notes
text:
A collection of best practices and common mistakes for technical writing at NPS — in particular for theses in the MAE department. These notes complement the official thesis guidelines and template; if there is any conflict in style recommendations, use the official NPS processing guidelines.
Ideally these will save you time, so you don’t have to fix known issues during the revision process.

title: Technical writing notes
text:
Contributions
The contributions of a thesis or research paper should be clear and concise. I recommend a subsection titled Contributions listing them in bullet form. There do not need to be many — one to three is typical — but they are critically important in guiding what evidence belongs in the work and what is left out. Everything in the document should relate to these points, helping you substantiate the claims.
Paraphrasing a colleague: “all research must answer a definitive question; good research answers an important question.” M. E. Swisher’s What Constitutes a Good Contribution provides worthwhile guidance.

title: Technical writing notes
text:
General grammar
If you don’t know how to use a particular grammatical construction, look it up rather than inventing your own usage. For example: when you use the word “but,” when should there be a preceding comma? There is a great deal of specific guidance online from many good sources.
For the basics — which cover 95% of what you need — I highly recommend Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style, available free online. Developing habits that follow the usage guidelines in this very short book will save you a lot of revision time.

title: Technical writing notes
text:
Figures and tables
There is a distinction between figure titles and captions:

The NPS thesis template puts figure titles below the image. As the template explains, figure titles are capitalized like a book title. This is what appears in the list of figures.
A figure caption is a brief explanation of the image contents, written in complete sentences and punctuated accordingly. The template formats these as Figure Secondary Caption. Captions are optional, but encouraged — a good portion of readers look at your figures and read the captions as the first step in reading your work.

Other rules that come up constantly:

All graphs should have labels on all axes, and the labels should include engineering units.
Any text in the figure — labels, legends — should use a font size similar to the document text and be clearly readable.
A common mistake is an image that carries its own title. For figures there should be no title inside the image (no title() command in MATLAB); the title belongs to the document.

See figures for writing for how to produce publication-quality images from MATLAB.

title: Technical writing notes
text:
Equations, numbers, and units






Important



These two aspects of thesis preparation are the most problematic.



Equations

Equations are grammatical elements within your document and should be punctuated accordingly.
See the ASME guidelines for how to reference equations in the text.
A Guide to Writing Mathematics, by Dr. Kevin P. Lee, is a good description of how to use equations in your text.



Numbers and units

Rules for the use of numbers in scientific writing — a succinct set of rules (Word version).
Use SI units, and use the abbreviation for the units when accompanying numerals.
Use a space between a number and its units: 0.5 m, not 0.5m.
When using a number less than 1.0, use a leading zero: 0.5 m, not .5 m.
Know the difference between a hyphen (-), an en dash (–), and an em dash (—). Use them correctly and know how to enter them in your typesetting software. Don’t use spaces before or after hyphens or dashes.

Hyphens connect compound terms: free-for-all.
En dashes are for ranges and can be read as through: 0.5–0.4 m.
Em dashes are for parenthetical expressions.


Guidelines for Equations, Units, and Mathematical Notation (Louisiana Tech University) is a good reference here — see in particular Section 4, “Numbers and units of measurement, in equations or anywhere in the document.”

title: Technical writing notes
text:
Style and citations
For issues not explicitly defined in the NPS template and style guide, the MAE department defaults to the ASME guidelines. Pay particular attention to the Equations and References sections.
Use ASME citation style, which is very similar to IEEE style.
For capitalization, see the Thesis Capitalization Rules under Style and Grammar in Thesis Processing: Resources.

title: MATLAB movie generation
text:
There are a few ways to generate movies, videos, and animations with MATLAB. Below is one method that works with Linux/Ubuntu. There are two basic steps:
The code for these examples is at github.com/bsb808/matlabmovie.

title: MATLAB movie generation
MATLAB movie generation
text:
Step 2: generating the movie
The following command finds those images and converts them into out.mp4:
avconv -framerate 4 -i "./movie/image-%05d.png" -c:v libx264 -r 20 \
  -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 20 \
  -vf "scale=trunc(iw/2)*2:trunc(ih/2)*2" out.mp4
The syntax is equivalent for ffmpeg. There are a number of cryptic options here.
If all goes well you have a movie:


The video quality here is not especially high. To improve it, adjust the image resolution in MATLAB, the command-line options to avconv/ffmpeg, or both.






Unlike a figure for a document, an animation of this kind reasonably carries its own title — note the title() call in the script above.

title: Figures for writing
text: Generating high-quality figures for documents — theses, papers — can be challenging. In general you will want to generate an image file from the figure window and then include that image in your document. Below are general notes with a Linux-specific example.

title: Figures for writing
text:
export_fig
The export_fig utility from the MathWorks File Exchange does most of the heavy lifting of saving high-resolution images from MATLAB figures. Download the zip archive and place it somewhere MATLAB can find the .m file — you can set the MATLAB path so that export_fig.m is always found.
Read the README and the File Information on File Exchange for documentation. In particular, you will need to install Ghostscript.

title: Figures for writing

MATLAB wrappers
Personally I get tired of typing all of that, or putting it in every script, so I have convenience functions for creating figures for publication. They live in the frlbox repository; the figure export scripts — pubfig.m and exfig.m — are in figbox.

title: Second reader expectations
text:
These notes are intended to manage bilateral expectations. In my experience, explicit expectations on both sides make things more efficient and more productive. Timing can be tight at the end of a student’s time at NPS, so part of the purpose here is to help you plan your thesis workflow schedule.
My approach as second reader is to support you in preparing a written thesis consistent with the expectations of the MAE Department, NPS, and the general engineering science academic community. Normally the second reader is not involved regularly with the research, though all NPS faculty are ready to help any student with domain-specific questions. If the second reader is expected to be a regular contributor to the research effort, it is probably more appropriate to modify the role to that of co-advisor.

title: Second reader expectations
text:
What I expect

You will review my technical writing notes before developing your final draft, and your draft will be free of the common mistakes addressed there.
I will be asked to review a final draft of your complete thesis document only after your advisor has reviewed and signed off on the document.
You will give me a minimum of one week’s notice of when to expect your completed draft.
You will send me the draft electronically as a PDF. Box or OneDrive is best for large files.
I will have at least one week to review the document and get it back to you. I will return it electronically with comments and edits.
Addressing the comments and edits can typically happen quickly, but you should plan time to make corrections.
I do not need to re-review the draft. I expect you will address all the comments, edits, and questions provided, and will ask for clarification if you need more detail on a specific issue.

title: Second reader expectations
text:
What you can expect

I will be available for specific questions while you work on your research and your thesis.
Once I have advance notice of when to expect your draft, I will block out a few hours to review it within one week — hopefully sooner.
I will return your draft with electronic notes. My opinions as second reader are secondary to your primary advisor’s guidance; if our recommendations conflict, follow your advisor.
Unless I say otherwise on the returned draft, we do not need to meet to go over the comments. They are intended to stand alone, and I assume you will address them all before submitting the final document.
If you have questions about the comments, or other follow-up questions, you can schedule time to work together to finalize the draft.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text: These are introductory notes for new and potential thesis advisees in the Field Robotics Lab. They exist to set expectations on both sides and to give you a schedule you can plan against. Explicit expectations make the work more efficient and more productive.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text:
What you are committing to






Important



To do a high-quality thesis requires that you commit to doing a thesis in FRL five quarters prior to your graduation.


Thesis research in FRL takes more time than the four thesis blocks allocated in your course matrix. The table below estimates the commitment in units of class blocks — roughly double the time formally allocated.

Course work and research work will often compete for your time. Courses should not be neglected for your research, but neither should your research be neglected for coursework. There will be times when you need to prioritize progress on your research over perfecting work for your courses.
NPS offers a number of additional educational opportunities — the TSSE program, FE/PE exam preparation, and others. In my experience, taking on these additional commitments should be carefully considered when planning your time.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text:
Generic thesis outline
For the purposes of this discussion, an NPS MS thesis consists of these chapters. This is an approximation, not a rule.

Introduction — motivation, problem statement, contributions.
Literature Review — background, closely related work.
Approach — background, procedures, methods, models, experimental setup.
Results and Analysis — the majority of the technical contribution.
Conclusion — discussion, summary referring back to the problem statement and contributions, and future work.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text:
The schedule
Typical deliverables by quarter follow. Your specific timeline will be based on your topic, but will likely vary only slightly.

Quarter 4: Background
Develop a specific thesis question and investigate the research literature to describe how your topic fits within the context of the current literature.
Mid-quarter:

Second Draft, thesis proposal
Outline of Literature Review chapter

End of quarter:

Final Draft, thesis proposal, including specific anticipated contributions
First Draft, Literature Review chapter, with document database and automated cross-references
Detailed Outline of Introduction



Quarter 3: Foundation
Acquire the knowledge and skills required to execute your approach. This may include reproducing previous results from the literature, learning new tools, or setting up new systems — vehicles, sensors, and so on.
Beginning of quarter:

Full Outline of Approach chapter

Mid-quarter:

First Draft of Introduction and Approach chapters

End of quarter:

Second Draft of Introduction and Approach chapters



Quarter 2: Execution
The culmination of the previous two quarters, and where the “doing” of the thesis work happens. By the end of the quarter you should have answered your thesis question.
Beginning of quarter:

Full Outline of Results and Analysis chapter

End of quarter:

90% of thesis research complete
Detailed Outline of Results and Analysis chapter



Quarter 1: Documentation
The emphasis shifts from doing the research to documenting the results. You begin by drafting the Results and Analysis chapter; assembling that material usually reveals additional work — experiments, simulations — needed to finalize the results. This is also when you begin working with the document as a whole rather than individual chapters.
Mid-quarter:

First Draft of Results and Analysis chapter
Detailed Outline of Conclusion chapter

End of quarter:

Second Draft of Results and Analysis chapter
First Draft of Conclusion chapter and Abstract
First Draft of complete thesis



Quarter 0: Graduation
This quarter guides your thesis through the revision and acceptance process.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text:
Writing
I provide notes and pointers to resources to help you prepare thesis documents, but I do not proofread your documents. When writing professional research documents — proposal, papers, thesis — you should:

Make sure you are prepared, by consulting the writing resources and doing whatever preparation you need in order to write effectively.
Prepare a First Draft.
Prepare a Second Draft by revising the document at least once, having at least one external person review it (a classmate, the graduate writing center), and revising again based on that review.


Stages of a document
I use these terms consistently when planning, so that we mean the same thing by them:







Stage
What it means




Outline
Headings, subheadings, and subsubheadings only.


Full Outline
Outline plus a description of each element — notes, bullet lists.


Detailed Outline
Full Outline plus key figures, tables, and equations, or sketches of what we expect them to look like. Includes bullet lists of anticipated results and conclusions.


First Draft
The first time the document is in a state to be reviewed and revised.


Second Draft
After you have revised it yourself, had it reviewed externally, and revised again based on that review. This is the draft that is ready for my review.


Third Draft
Reviewed by me and revised — ready for the second reader.


Final Draft
Accepted by the second reader and ready for department review.



The Full Outline and Detailed Outline are the critical steps. Once we agree on the Detailed Outline for each part of your thesis, the writing itself should be fairly straightforward.

title: MS Thesis Advising Quickstart
text:
How my review works






Important



My review happens between the Second and Third Drafts, and at least three weeks should be budgeted for it. That allows time for iteration, discussion, and the possibility of additional experiments and analysis.


My detailed review is done on the complete thesis document at the Second Draft stage, including complete conclusions and abstract. I am of course happy to review parts of the document earlier — a specific chapter or section you have questions about — but reviewing the complete document is the most efficient use of everyone’s time.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text: A few high-level, general notes on preparing and delivering your master’s thesis brief.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text:
Audience and objective
Your audience is the NPS faculty and your Program Officer, so you can assume general technical knowledge and an understanding of Naval priorities.
Your objective is to communicate a succinct description of your research contributions and substantiate those contributions with evidence.






Tip



A thought experiment. The Department Chair attends your presentation along with three others. Afterward they go to Starbucks and run into the GSEAS Dean, who asks, “You just came from LT X’s thesis presentation, true? What was their research about?” The Chair should be able to summarize, from memory, what you have worked on for the last 12–18 months.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text:
Highlight your contributions
Early in the presentation, include a Contributions slide that lays them out clearly in bullet points.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text:
It won’t all fit
You cannot fit your entire thesis into a 15-minute brief.

Start with your contributions, and include the findings, conclusions, and results you feel are most important, compelling, or interesting.
Focus on the results more than the process that led to them — but be prepared to defend both the process and the evidence.
Significant parts of your thesis will have to be left out. Two strategies help:

It is fine to allude to detail that lives in the document: “the derivation of this expression is in the thesis, but I’m not going to cover it here.”
Include backup slides for aspects likely to come up in questions.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text:
Timing
Plan for a 15-minute brief, with 5 minutes for questions and transition.

title: MS thesis presentation guidelines
text:
Preparation

Start with an outline to decide what to include and what to leave out. Reviewing the outline with your advisor before building slides is suggested, though not required.
Practice alone first, for timing. Practice like you play — stand up, speak out loud, and use a stopwatch.
Then practice with an audience of your advisor(s) and peers. Schedule this at least two days before your brief so you have time to revise.
